'''Nicholas G. Blurton-Jones''' (1938 – 8 June 2026) was a British [[biologist]] and [[evolutionary anthropologist]] known for his extensive [[Ethnography|ethnographic]] research on [[child development]], the [[Grandmother hypothesis]], and the [[Human behavioral ecology|behavioral ecology]] of modern [[Hunter-gatherer|foragers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Remembering Nicholas Blurton-Jones {{!}} Center for Academic Research and Training in Anthropogeny (CARTA) |url=https://carta.anthropogeny.org/blog/remembering-nicholas-blurton-jones |access-date=2026-08-22 |website=carta.anthropogeny.org |language=en}}</ref> He was a Professor Emeritus in the Departments of Psychiatry and Anthropology at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], and earlier the Department of Growth and Development at the [[UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health|Institute of Child Health]] (ICH), [[UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health|Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children]], which later [[UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health#History|merged]] with [[University College London]]. In 2021, he was elected a [[Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science|Fellow]] of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in the Section of Anthropology, for his contributions to the field.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Four professors named fellows of the American Association for the Advancement of Science |url=https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/four-professors-named-fellows-of-the-american-association-for-the-advancement-of-science |access-date=2026-08-22 |website=UCLA |language=en-us}}</ref> 

==Early life and education==
Blurton-Jones was born in [[Weymouth, Dorset|Weymouth Parish]], [[Dorset]] in 1936.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nicholas Blurton-Jones |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q107783920 |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=www.wikidata.org |language=en}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=October 2026}} He attended [[Leighton Park School]], where he first acquired an interest in [[ornithology]] after joining a [[Birdwatching|birdwatching club]] organized by the school's [[Botany|botanist]] headmaster, John Ounsted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Akeroyd |first=J.R. |date=2008 |title='Obituaries', Watsonia 27, 199-206 |url=http://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Wats27p199.pdf |format=PDF |journal=Watsonia |volume=27 |pages=199–206 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240329101357/http://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Wats27p199.pdf |archive-date=2024-03-29}}</ref> In 1954 he enrolled at the [[University of Reading]], pursuing a BSc with a focus in Zoology, Botany, and Psychology. During the summer before his first year at university, he performed the first field census on [[Canada goose|Canadian geese]] for the [[Edward Grey Institute of Field Ornithology]], in the [[Department of Zoology, University of Oxford|Department of Zoology]] at the [[University of Oxford]]. The project was funded by a grant from the [[British Trust for Ornithology]], and the young Blurton-Jones was assisted by the ornithologists [[Peter Scott]] and [[Wilfrid Backhouse Alexander]], the Institute's director at the time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jones |first=N. G. Blurton |date=1956-09-01 |title=Census of Breeding Canada Geese 1953 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00063655609475845 |journal=Bird Study |publisher=Taylor & Francis |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=153–170 |doi=10.1080/00063655609475845 |issn=0006-3657}}</ref> The report was published in 1955. 

Blurton-Jones received his BSc in 1958<ref name="webteam1">{{Cite web |last=webteam |date=2020-08-05 |title=Nicholas Blurton-Jones |url=https://anthro.ucla.edu/person/nicholas-blurton-jones/ |access-date=2026-10-25 |website=UCLA Department of Anthropology |language=en-US}}</ref> and stayed on in the Department of Zoology, starting a PhD under the Dutch biologist [[Nikolaas Tinbergen]] in the ornithology group of the British [[Evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]] and [[Ethology|ethologist]] [[David Lack]], the Department's director at the time. Blurton-Jones' thesis fieldwork on the [[Deimatic behaviour|threat displays]] of [[Great tit|''Parus major'']] while under Tinbergen are part of the body of contributions for which the latter shared the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine#Laureates|1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] with the ethologists [[Karl von Frisch]] and [[Konrad Lorenz]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jones |first=N. G. Blurton |date=1968-01-01 |title=Observations and Experiments on Causation of Threat Displays of the Great Tit (Parus major) |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0066185668800020 |journal=Animal Behaviour Monographs |volume=1 |pages=73–158 |doi=10.1016/S0066-1856(68)80002-0 |issn=0066-1856}}</ref> He successfully defended his PhD in 1961.<ref name="webteam1" />

== Career and research ==
In 1960, while still working under Tinbergen, Blurton-Jones had a chance conversation with Eileen Molony and the British conservationist [[John Burton (conservationist)|John Burton]] while visiting the [[BBC Studios Natural History Unit|BBC Natural History Unit]]. The two suggested that ethologists should verge into studying human behavior, particularly that of young children in the relatively controlled environment of nursery school. He then arranged access to suitable facility through the College of Further Education in Oxford, and after several interruptions involving ethnographic fieldwork with indigenous foragers in Africa, ended up in the [[UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health|Institute of Child Health]] (ICH), at the time the largest center for children's health research in Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Driscoll |first=David |title=Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health |url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/population-health-sciences/child-health |access-date=2026-08-22 |website=Faculty of Population Health Sciences |language=en}}</ref> He established a childhood development research lab under the department of pediatrician [[James Mourilyan Tanner]], who had sought an ethologist for such a project.<ref name="Blurton Jones1">{{Cite book |last=Blurton Jones |first=N. G. (Nicholas G. ) |url=http://archive.org/details/ethologicalstudi00blur |title=Ethological Studies of Child Behaviour |date=1972 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-521-08260-0 |page=X}}</ref>
[[File:Institute of Child Health, Guilford Street - geograph.org.uk - 7222689.jpg|thumb|391x391px|The [[UCL Great Ormond Street Institute of Child Health|Institute for Child Health]], at [[Great Ormond Street Hospital|Great Ormond Street Children's Hospital]] in [[London]].]]
Blurton-Jones' first work on foragers was with the [[San peoples|San people]] of the [[Kalahari Desert|Kalahari desert]] in modern [[Botswana]], in collaboraiton with the anthropologist [[Melvin Konner]], who began studying the child raising practices of San communities during the same period.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Monmaney |first=Terence |title=Melvin Konner on the Evolution of Childhood |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/melvin-konner-on-the-evolution-of-childhood-904697/ |access-date=2026-10-25 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref> During this period Blurton-Jones explored the use of formal evolutionary modeling of [[child development]], [[kinship]], and cross-cultural study of [[Parental investment#Parental investment in humans|parent-child interactions]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nicholas Blurton-Jones {{!}} Center for Academic Research and Training in Anthropogeny (CARTA) |url=https://carta.anthropogeny.org/users/nicholas-blurton-jones |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=carta.anthropogeny.org |language=en}}</ref> Notably, he also published comparisons between modern foraging communities such as the [[Hadza people|Hadza]] of [[Tanzania]]<ref name="OConnell1988">{{Cite journal |last1=O'Connell |first1=James F. |last2=Hawkes |first2=Kristen |last3=Jones |first3=Nicholas Blurton |title=Hadza Hunting, Butchering, and Bone Transport and Their Archaeological Implications |journal=Journal of Anthropological Research |date=1988 |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=113–161 |doi=10.1086/jar.44.2.3630053}}</ref> and the [[ǃKung]] of the [[Kalahari desert]] with urban populations in [[London]], including his work on children at the ICH.

=== Development of evolutionary demography ===
In 1979, while a senior lecturer at the ICH, Blurton-Jones and British evolutionary biologist Richard Sibly applied evolutionary modeling to extensive ethnographic data on the !Kung produced by Harvard anthropologists [[Richard Borshay Lee]] and [[Nancy Howell Lee]], particularly claims by the latter regarding [[birth spacing]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jones |first=Nicholas Blurton |date=1986-01-01 |title=Bushman birth spacing: A test for optimal interbirth intervals |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0162-3095%2886%2990002-6 |journal=Ethology and Sociobiology |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=91–105 |doi=10.1016/0162-3095(86)90002-6 |issn=0162-3095}}</ref> In one of the first evolutionary demographic (later also called [[biodemography]]) studies, they modeled how selection acts on birth spacing as a function of resource scarcity in women practicing foraging lifestyles, and their results (and the modeling approach more generally) are now referred to as Blurton-Jones's ‘backload model’.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sear |first1=Rebecca |last2=Lawson |first2=David W. |last3=Kaplan |first3=Hillard |last4=Shenk |first4=Mary K. |date=2016-04-19 |title=Understanding variation in human fertility: what can we learn from evolutionary demography? |url=https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2015.0144 |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |volume=371 |issue=1692 |article-number=20150144 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2015.0144 |pmid=27022071 |pmc=4822424 |issn=0962-8436}}</ref> The study was inspired by his time working under Lack,<ref>{{Cite book |editor-first1=Oskar |editor-first2=Ronald |editor-first3=Rebecca |editor-last1=Burger |editor-last2=Lee |editor-last3=Sear |title=Human Evolutionary Demography - 8. Why Do We Do What We Do? Analysing the Evolutionary Function of Reproductive Behaviour |date=2024 |doi=10.11647/obp.0251 |doi-access=free |isbn=978-1-80064-170-9 }}</ref> who famously first modeled bird [[Clutch (eggs)#Size|clutch sizes]] (i.e., the number of eggs laid together in a group) as [[Functional response|response curves]], maximizing the average number of surviving offpsring in a clutch as a function of available resources. The resulting conclusion is that [[natural selection]] will favor lineages who balance between not producing enough offspring to take full advantage of available resources, and producing too many eggs such that some offspring perish before maturity, wasting the [[Parental investment|energetic investment of reproduction]]. This model has been generalized to a [[Biological rules|biological rule]] known as [[Lack's principle]] and was a significant step in the [[history of evolutionary thought]]. It is commonly considered to have sparked the debate between [[group selection]] (originated from figures such as [[V. C. Wynne-Edwards]]) and the [[History of evolutionary thought#Gene-centered view|gene-centered view of evolution]], the latter of which has generally reached consensus.

=== Ethnography on Hadza communities ===
Along with American anthropologists and long-time collaborators [[Kristen Hawkes]] and [[James F. O'Connell]], Blurton-Jones co-authored many scientific papers on the social and behavioral ecology of Hadza communities, including analyses of [[Sexual division of labour|sexual division of labor]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=O'Connell |first1=James |last2=Hawkes |first2=Kristen |last3=Jones |first3=Nicholas Blurton |date=2024-05-01 |title=Hadza Men's Follows, 1985-1986: Data and Implications for Ideas About Ancestral Male Foraging Effort in Human Evolution |url=https://paleoanthropology.org/ojs/index.php/paleo/article/view/1084 |journal=PaleoAnthropology |language=en |volume=2024 |issue=1 |pages=112–138 |doi=10.48738/2024.iss1.1084 |issn=1545-0031}}</ref> the cost of pregnancy and childrearing,<ref>{{Citation |last1=Blurton-Jones |first1=Nicholas |title=Modeling and measuring the costs of children in two foraging societies |date=1989-01-01 |work=Comparative Socioecology: The Behavioural Ecology of Humans and Other Mammals |pages=367–390 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/293817737 |access-date=2026-08-22 |last2=Hawkes |first2=Kristen |last3=O'Connell |first3=James}}</ref> strategies of butchering and the archaeology of faunal assemblages,<ref name="OConnell1988" /> and the social life history of Hadza women.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hawkes |first1=K. |last2=O'Connell |first2=J. F. |last3=Blurton Jones |first3=N. G. |date=August 1997 |title=Hadza Women's Time Allocation, Offspring Provisioning, and the Evolution of Long Postmenopausal Life Spans |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/204646 |journal=Current Anthropology |volume=38 |issue=4 |pages=551–577 |doi=10.1086/204646 |bibcode=1997CurrA..38..551H }}</ref>

His 2016 book ''Demography and Evolutionary Ecology of Hadza Hunter-Gatherers'' covers over 16 years of fieldwork with the Hadza from Blurton-Jones as well as Hawkes and O'Connell, and is considered a major work in modern anthropological ethnography and a reference for [[Cross-cultural studies|cross-cultural anthropology]]. In addition to fieldwork, also contains a systematic literature review going back to ethnographies of the early 20th century.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Blurton Jones |first=Nicholas |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/demography-and-evolutionary-ecology-of-hadza-huntergatherers/57B133BBAED33BC9231410D6A91794BD |title=Demography and Evolutionary Ecology of Hadza Hunter-Gatherers |date=2016 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-06982-4 |series=Cambridge Studies in Biological and Evolutionary Anthropology |location=Cambridge |doi=10.1017/CBO9781107707030}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pontzer |first=Herman |date=2017-11-01 |title=DEMOGRAPHY AND EVOLUTIONARY ECOLOGY OF HADZA HUNTER-GATHERERS By Nicholas Blurton Jones 508 pp. (2016). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. $130.00 (paperback) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ajhb.23053 |journal=American Journal of Human Biology |language=en |volume=29 |issue=6 |article-number=e23053 |doi=10.1002/ajhb.23053 |issn=1520-6300}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Borgerhoff Mulder |first=Monique |date=2017-03-01 |title=Review of Demography and Evolutionary Ecology of Hadza Hunter-Gatherers by Nicholas Blurton Jones |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s12110-016-9280-9 |journal=Human Nature |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=117–127 |doi=10.1007/s12110-016-9280-9 |issn=1936-4776}}</ref>

== Contributions to evolutionary anthropology ==

=== Ethology and the development of modern behavioral ecology ===
{{Main|Human behavioral ecology}}
Along with Tinbergen and other biologists he mentored such as [[Richard Dawkins]], [[John Krebs, Baron Krebs|John Krebs]], and [[Tim Clutton-Brock]], Blurton-Jones contributed to the synthesis of the modern biological study of behavior from several related and preceding approaches, such as ethology. Primarily, this contribution was through his introduction of mathematical modeling of [[natural selection]] in studies of human behavior, development, and reproduction, which have since become standard in such research.<ref name="Stuhrmann2022">{{Cite journal |last=Stuhrmann |first=Cora |date=2022 |title="It Felt More like a Revolution." How Behavioral Ecology Succeeded Ethology, 1970–1990 |journal=Berichte zur Wissenschaftsgeschichte |language=en |volume=45 |issue=1–2 |pages=135–163 |doi=10.1002/bewi.202200002 |issn=1522-2365 |pmc=9321734 |pmid=35467771}}</ref> This realm was a major interest of Tinbergen's, which he described and partially predicted in 1963:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tinbergen |first=N. |date=1963-01-12 |title=On aims and methods of Ethology |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1439-0310.1963.tb01161.x |journal=Zeitschrift für Tierpsychologie |language=en |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=410–433 |doi=10.1111/j.1439-0310.1963.tb01161.x |bibcode=1963Ethol..20..410T |issn=0044-3573}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barrett |first1=Louise |last2=Blumstein |first2=Daniel T. |last3=Clutton-Brock |first3=Timothy H. |last4=Kappeler |first4=Peter M. |date=2013-05-19 |title=Taking note of Tinbergen, or: the promise of a biology of behaviour |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological Sciences |volume=368 |issue=1618 |article-number=20120352 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2012.0352 |issn=1471-2970 |pmc=3638455 |pmid=23569300}}</ref>

{{Quote
| quote = ... the thesis that we are witnessing [is] the fusing of many sciences, all concerned with one or another aspect of behaviour into one coherent science, for which the only correct name is ‘Biology of Behaviour'
| author = Tinbergen
| source = p. 430
|title=''On aims and methods of Ethology''}}Traditionally, ethology is considered to have split into [[sociobiology]] and behavioral ecology, the former instigated by the American evolutionary biologist [[E. O. Wilson]] with his 1975 book, ''Sociobiology: The New Synthesis''.<ref name="Stuhrmann2022" /> Here, "new synthesis" refers to an ostensible successor to the [[Modern synthesis (20th century)|modern synthesis]] of evolutionary biology, which fused several related scientific topics such as [[population genetics]], [[natural selection]], and [[Mendelian inheritance]]. Wilson's book sparked a [[Modern synthesis (20th century)#Wilson's sociobiology, 1975|yet-unresolved debate]] among scientists and in popular discourse, and from the start the term was often avoided in public forums and especially when applied to human populations. In particular, accusations of [[Biological determinism|biological essentialism]] and [[scientific racism]] were levied against Wilson by groups such as [[Science for the People]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stuhrmann |first1=Cora |last2=Ghosh |first2=Nayanika |date=2025-02-01 |title=No End in Sight: The Sociobiology Debate at Fifty |url=https://doi.org/10.1525/hsns.2025.55.1.37 |journal=Historical Studies in the Natural Sciences |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=37–43 |doi=10.1525/hsns.2025.55.1.37 |issn=1939-1811}}</ref> Behavioral ecology (and by extension [[human behavioral ecology]]) became the generally preferred terms, and today represent the majority self-identification of researchers in this realm. Blurton-Jones generally referred to his approaches as behavioral or social ecology, bringing human cultural traits into the scope of analysis as ecological effects in [[human evolution]] and [[paleoanthropology]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stuhrmann |first=Cora |date=June 2022 |title="It Felt More like a Revolution." How Behavioral Ecology Succeeded Ethology, 1970–1990 |journal=Berichte zur Wissenschaftsgeschichte |language=de |volume=45 |issue=1–2 |pages=135–163 |doi=10.1002/bewi.202200002 |issn=0170-6233 |pmc=9321734 |pmid=35467771}}</ref>

Tinbergen discussed the topic further in the [[Foreword|foreward]] to Blurton-Jones' scientific reference text, ''Ethological Studies of Child Behavior'' (1972):<ref name="Blurton Jones1" />
{{Blockquote|text=As I was reading the variety of studies on which the book reports (many of which I had until recently been following only from a distance), I was increasingly reminded of the early days of animal ethology, and I felt that what is now just beginning to happen in human ethology is reminiscent of what occurred in the later 'twenties and early 'thirties to the science of animal behaviour; a new type of research worker is busy building the foundations of a science, by returning, with renewed attention and interest in detail, to the basic task of observation and description of the natural phenomena that have to be understood. I call this 'building' because, with due respect to human psychology in its widest sense, I consider that it is not yet really a science.}}
In January 1977, Blurton-Jones chaired an important symposium for the [[Society for the Study of Human Biology]] at [[St Antony's College, Oxford|St. Antony's College, Oxford]], along with the British anthropologist [[Vernon Reynolds]]. It was the Society's first meeting on the topic of human behavior in an evolutionary context, and was funded by the [[Nuffield Foundation]] and the [[Royal Society]] which allowed for a large number of presentations from leading biologists, zoologists, and psychologists at the time, including [[William H. Durham]], [[Andrew P. Vayda]], [[Bonnie McCay]], [[David McFarland|David J. McFarland]], [[Roy Rappaport]], [[Craig Packer]], [[David R. Harris (geographer)|David R. Harris]], [[:sv:Töres_Theorell|Töres Theorell]], [[Mary Carruthers]], and [[Gunnar Johansson (psychophysicist)|Gunnar Johansson]]. The authors presented various positions on their own clinical and ethnographic research, as well as discussions of the developing nature and methods of behavioral ecology at the time. Blurton-Jones published the proceedings the following year in a volume entitled ''Human Behavior and Adaptation''.<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://archive.org/details/humanbehaviourad0000unse |title=Human behaviour and adaptation |date=1978 |publisher=London : Taylor & Francis ; New York : distributed by Halsted Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-85066-137-8}}</ref>

Since the 1970s, various related subdisciplines specific to human behavior have arisen and interacted in various ways, such as [[Dual inheritance theory|gene-culture coevolution]] (also known as "dual-inheritance theory" or DIT), [[cultural evolution]], and [[evolutionary psychology]].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Brown |first1=Gillian R. |title=Sense and nonsense |date=2024-12-13 |work=Sense and Nonsense: Evolutionary Perspectives on Human Behaviour |pages=0 |editor-last=Brown |editor-first=Gillian R. |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198908203.003.0001 |access-date=2026-08-22 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-890820-3 |last2=Lala |first2=Kevin N. |doi=10.1093/oso/9780198908203.003.0001 |editor2-last=Lala |editor2-first=Kevin N.}}</ref> The latter has faced the most criticism, especially accusations of "[[Just-so story|just-so stories]]" and a pervasive lack of empirical rigor by figures such as [[David Sloan Wilson]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=David Sloan |date=2002-11-01 |title=Human Evolutionary Psychology: Pardon Our Dust |url=https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0014-3820.2002.tb00157.x |journal=Evolution |volume=56 |issue=11 |pages=2334–2338 |doi=10.1111/j.0014-3820.2002.tb00157.x |issn=0014-3820}}</ref> In 1990, Blurton-Jones reviewed some of the competing approaches and, like Sloan Wilson, offered a critique of evolutionary psychology (then referred to as "Darwinian psychology") as lacking an empirical basis for investigation:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Blurton Jones |first=Nicholas G. |date=1990-07-01 |title=Three sensible paradigms for research on evolution and human behavior? |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0162-3095%2890%2990015-X |journal=Ethology and Sociobiology |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=353–359 |doi=10.1016/0162-3095(90)90015-X |issn=0162-3095}}</ref>
[[File:San Schmuck.JPG|thumb|417x417px|[[Cultural learning]] is vital to human survival, and older individuals play an important role in this process across all cultures.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barone |first=Francine |date=2024-03-12 |title=Status and Role of the Elderly (Explaining Human Culture) {{!}} Human Relations Area Files |url=https://hraf.yale.edu/teach-ehraf/status-and-role-of-the-elderly-explaining-human-culture/ |access-date=2026-08-25}}</ref>]]
{{Blockquote|text=the biggest challenge to Darwinian psychologists is certainly not establishing their claim to a logically meaningful place in our field (they have one) but showing us what they are going to do, and how, and just doing it.|author=Blurton-Jones|title=''Three sensible paradigms for research on evolution and human behavior?''}}
=== Grandmother hypothesis ===
{{Main|Grandmother hypothesis}}
The [[grandmother hypothesis]] is a conjecture which relates the relatively dramatic [[Life history theory#Human life history|post-reproductive lifespan]] of humans to increased survival of children (especially infants) as well as the transmission of [[cultural learning]]. In this way, it is considered a subtype of [[cooperative breeding]] possibly unique to humans,<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2017-07-28 |title=Comes the Child before Man : How Cooperative Breeding and Prolonged Postweaning Dependence Shaped Human Potential |url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9780203789445-4/comes-child-man-sarah-blaffer-hrdy |journal=Taylor & Francis |language=en |doi=10.4324/9780203789445-4 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240415100927/https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9780203789445-4/comes-child-man-sarah-blaffer-hrdy |archive-date=2024-04-15}}</ref> and is one of the most important theoretical problems in the study of [[Life history theory#Human life history|human life history evolution]]. While unique to humans in proportion of total lifespan, both menopause and significant post-menopausal lifespan have been documented in social mammals including chimpanzees,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wood |first1=Brian M. |last2=Negrey |first2=Jacob D. |last3=Brown |first3=Janine L. |last4=Deschner |first4=Tobias |last5=Thompson |first5=Melissa Emery |last6=Gunter |first6=Sholly |last7=Mitani |first7=John C. |last8=Watts |first8=David P. |last9=Langergraber |first9=Kevin E. |date=2023-10-27 |title=Demographic and hormonal evidence for menopause in wild chimpanzees |journal=Science |volume=382 |issue=6669 |article-number=eadd5473 |doi=10.1126/science.add5473 |pmc=10645439 |pmid=37883540 |bibcode=2023Sci...382d5473W }}</ref> and has independently evolved at least four times in [[Toothed whale|toothed whales]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ellis |first1=Samuel |last2=Franks |first2=Daniel W. |last3=Nielsen |first3=Mia Lybkær Kronborg |last4=Weiss |first4=Michael N. |last5=Croft |first5=Darren P. |date=March 2024 |title=The evolution of menopause in toothed whales |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=627 |issue=8004 |pages=579–585 |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-07159-9 |pmid=38480878 |pmc=10954554 |bibcode=2024Natur.627..579E |issn=1476-4687}}</ref>

Alongside decades of collaboration with Hawkes and O'Connell, Blurton-Jones contributed to the field ethnography and the development and mathematical formalizing of the grandmother hypothesis, introducing evolutionary concepts such as [[kin selection]] and [[inclusive fitness]] to parameterize the broad but largely unstructured idea.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hawkes |first1=K. |last2=O'Connell |first2=J.F |last3=Blurton-Jones |first3=N.G. |date=1989 |title=Hardworking Hadza grandmothers |url=https://content.csbs.utah.edu/~hawkes/Hawkes_al89hardworkingHadzaGrams.pdf |journal=Comparative Socioecology}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2005-08-10 |title=Grandmotherhood |url=https://www.rutgersuniversitypress.org/grandmotherhood/9780813571416 |access-date=2026-08-22 |website=www.rutgersuniversitypress.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Voland |first=Eckart |title=Altern und Lebenslauf – ein evolutionsbiologischer Aufriss1 |date=2009 |work=Generationen: Multidisziplinäre Perspektiven |pages=23–43 |editor-last=Künemund |editor-first=Harald |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-531-91499-2_2 |access-date=2026-08-22 |place=Wiesbaden |publisher=VS Verlag
